title: Factory Method Pattern
tagline: Decouple object creation from usage by letting subclasses decide which class to instantiate — the cornerstone of the 'program to an interface, not an implementation' principle.

sections.content:
Imagine you are building a document-export library. Version 1 only exports PDFs, so you write `new PdfExporter()` throughout your code. Six months later the product team wants Word exports. Now you must hunt down every `new PdfExporter()` call and replace or branch it — touching a dozen files, risking regressions, violating the rule that existing, working code should not have to change just because you are *adding* something new.

This is the **object-creation problem** at the heart of the Factory Method pattern. Every time you hardcode a constructor call with `new ConcreteClass()` inside business logic, you are coupling two concerns that should be separate: *what work to do* and *which object to use while doing it*. When the object changes, the work logic must change too — and that is the coupling that hurts.

**The Factory Method pattern** solves this by defining an interface (a *factory method*) for creating an object, but delegating the decision of *which* concrete class to instantiate to a subclass or a separate creator. The creator's business logic calls `this.createProduct()` and receives back a `Product` interface it can use — oblivious to whether it got a PdfExporter, WordExporter, or HtmlExporter. Adding a new export format means adding a new subclass, not editing anything that already works.

This pattern is one of the original 23 Gang of Four (GoF) creational patterns, but its influence goes far beyond a textbook technique. It underlies React's component model, Node's `http.createServer`, NestJS module factories, Angular's `ComponentFactory`, and virtually every plugin or middleware system you have ever used. Understanding Factory Method at depth means understanding *why* frameworks are designed the way they are.

In this chapter you will study: the problem space in concrete terms, the four structural participants and their responsibilities, how the pattern satisfies the Open/Closed Principle using polymorphism, the difference between Factory Method and simple factory (a common conflation), the natural synergy with the Template Method pattern, idiomatic JavaScript and TypeScript implementations including the registry approach, real framework examples, edge cases, misconceptions, and when the pattern is overkill.

sections.caption: The classic Factory Method class diagram. Creator declares the factory method returning a Product interface. Concrete subclasses decide which ConcreteProduct to instantiate. Client code depends only on Creator and Product — never on the concrete classes themselves.

sections.title: A Staffing Agency That Specialises
sections.content:
Picture a company that needs workers for different roles. Rather than hiring directly, it contracts with Staffing Agencies. The company calls the agency and says 'send me a worker' — it does not care about the agency's internal sourcing process. One agency specialises in software engineers; another in accountants; a third in legal staff. Each agency's `hireWorker()` method is the factory method. The company (the client) codes against the 'worker can do their job' interface, never against 'this specific person with this specific hiring history'.

When the company needs a fourth type of worker — say, a data analyst — it does not change its internal processes. It simply signs with a new DataAnalystAgency. The existing code for deploying engineers, accountants, and lawyers is untouched. The company is **open for extension** (a new agency) but **closed for modification** (no changes to how it calls `agency.hireWorker()`).

This captures exactly what Factory Method does: it moves the 'which concrete thing' decision out of the user code and into an interchangeable creator, so extending the system means *adding*, not *editing*.

sections.title: The Problem in Detail: Why Hard-Coded Construction Hurts
The Four Participants and Their Contracts
sections.content:
The Factory Method pattern has four precisely defined roles:

**Product** is the interface (or abstract base class) that defines the behaviour all created objects must support. This is what the Creator codes against. Defining a clean Product interface is the most important design decision — if the interface is too narrow, Concrete Products cannot vary meaningfully; if it is too broad, implementors are burdened with irrelevant methods.

**ConcreteProduct** implements the Product interface for a specific variant. There is one ConcreteProduct per 'flavour' the system supports. `FileLogger`, `StdoutLogger`, `DatabaseLogger` are all ConcreteProducts of the `Logger` interface. Each knows its own construction details (file paths, connection strings, etc.) that the Creator should never need to know.

**Creator** is the class that declares the factory method `createProduct(): Product`. Critically, the Creator's *other* methods — its business logic — are implemented entirely in terms of the Product interface. When `LogManager.log()` calls `this.createLogger()`, it gets back a Logger interface and calls `.write()` — it never inspects the concrete type. The Creator may optionally provide a default implementation of the factory method (returning a sensible default product), making it an abstract method is stricter but forces concrete subclasses.

**ConcreteCreator** extends Creator and overrides `createProduct()` to return an instance of one specific ConcreteProduct. `FileLogManager` overrides to return `new FileLogger(...)`. It may receive configuration parameters in its constructor — these become part of how it builds its product. The ConcreteCreator knows *one thing*: which concrete product it is responsible for.

**The client's view:** client code receives a Creator reference (often via dependency injection) and calls business operations on it. The client is unaware of which ConcreteCreator or ConcreteProduct is active. This is the decoupling that makes the pattern valuable — the client is shielded from all construction details.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as "Client"
    participant CR as "ConcreteCreator"
    participant CP as "ConcreteProduct"

sections.title: Simple Factory vs Factory Method: A Critical Distinction

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: `processDocuments` is the client. It calls `.batchConvert()` on whatever `DocumentConverter` it receives — it has no idea whether that is a PdfConverter, HtmlConverter, or MarkdownConverter. Adding EPUB support requires only two new classes at the bottom; every existing class, every existing test, every existing call to `processDocuments` is completely unaffected. That is the Open/Closed Principle delivered by polymorphism.

sections.title: Factory Method and the Template Method Pattern

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Client calls\nconverter.convert(doc)"] --> B["Template: log start"]
    B --> C["Hook: createExporter()"]
    C --> D{"Which subclass?"}
    D --> E["PdfConverter\nreturns PdfExporter"]
    D --> F["HtmlConverter\nreturns HtmlExporter"]
    E --> G["Template: exporter.export(doc)"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["Template: wrap result"]
    H --> I["Return to client"]
sections.caption: The Template Method (convert) calls the Factory Method hook (createExporter). Subclasses only override the hook — the template steps execute identically for every creator. The two patterns are naturally intertwined.

sections.title: Idiomatic JavaScript: The Registry Pattern

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The registry is the idiomatic JS approach to Factory Method. `AppLogger` delegates product creation to `createLogger()` — it never uses `new RemoteLogger()` directly. Adding the `RemoteLogger` requires zero edits to any existing code: one `registerLogger` call is all it takes. The `NullLogger` illustrates a practical benefit: in tests, you swap the logger type string and get silent behaviour without mocking infrastructure.

sections.title: TypeScript: Typing the Factory Method Correctly

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Simple Factory\nswitch on type string"] --> B["Must edit\nfor new types"]
    C["Factory Method\noverride createProduct()"] --> D["Add subclass\nfor new types"]
    E["Registry Pattern\nregisterFactory(key, fn)"] --> F["Register new entry\nfor new types"]
    B --> G["OCP violated"]
    D --> H["OCP satisfied"]
    F --> H
sections.caption: Three approaches to the creation problem. Simple factory requires editing existing code (violates OCP). Factory Method and the registry both allow extension without modification (satisfy OCP) — they differ in mechanism but share the same principle.

sections.title: Real Frameworks That Use Factory Method
sections.content:
Once you know the pattern, you will see it everywhere in production frameworks.

**React's createElement:** JSX compiles `<MyButton color='blue'>Click</MyButton>` to `React.createElement(MyButton, { color: 'blue' }, 'Click')`. `createElement` is a factory method — it creates React element descriptors (the Product) without the caller needing to know how element objects are structured internally. When React introduced Fiber, the internal Product structure changed completely, but no JSX code needed updating because it all went through the factory.

**Node.js http module:** `http.createServer(handler)` is a factory method. It returns an `http.Server` instance (the Product). You pass it a handler and call `.listen()` — you never construct an `http.Server` with `new`. The factory encapsulates all the socket initialisation, SSL option handling, and platform-specific TCP binding. On Windows and Linux the internals differ; the factory method hides that entirely.

**NestJS providers:** NestJS's dependency injection system uses factory providers: `{ provide: 'CONFIG', useFactory: () => loadConfig() }`. The `useFactory` is a factory method — the container calls it at startup to produce the Product (the config object). It can be async, it can depend on other injected values, it can vary by environment. The consumer just injects `'CONFIG'` and gets a fully-built object.

**Angular's ComponentFactory:** `ComponentFactoryResolver.resolveComponentFactory(MyComponent)` returns a `ComponentFactory` — a Creator. Calling `factory.create(injector)` is the factory method that produces a live component instance. Dynamic component loading in Angular is entirely built on this pattern.

**Jest's `jest.fn()` and `jest.spyOn()`:** `jest.fn()` is a factory that returns a mock function (the Product). Every mock starts identically from the creator's perspective; the implementation (return values, side effects) is configured on the product after creation. This separation of construction from configuration is Factory Method applied to testing infrastructure.

**Mongoose's `model()`:** `mongoose.model('User', schema)` is a factory method that creates a Model class (the Product) from a schema. The returned Model class knows how to query MongoDB for User documents. You never construct a Model manually — the factory does it, hiding the connection, schema compilation, and plugin registration.

sections.caption: Decision tree for choosing among simple factory, Factory Method, and the registry. Start by asking whether the type set is closed or open-ended, then decide whether a class hierarchy is warranted.

sections.content: **Factory Method in the GoF taxonomy:** Factory Method is classified as a *creational pattern* that operates at the *class level* (using inheritance), distinguishing it from Abstract Factory, which operates at the *object level* (using composition). Abstract Factory groups related factory methods into one interface — you can think of Abstract Factory as a 'family of factory methods'. If Factory Method is one door, Abstract Factory is a building with multiple matched doors. Many systems start with Factory Method and evolve to Abstract Factory when they need to create *families* of related products that must be consistent with each other (e.g., a 'dark theme' that produces DarkButton, DarkInput, DarkDropdown all at once).

**When to use Factory Method:**
- You are building a framework or library with extension points — your code needs to create objects but users should control which concrete class gets created
- You have scattered `new ConcreteClass()` calls in business logic that make testing difficult (because you cannot substitute the concrete class)
- You see `switch (type) { case ... return new ... }` appearing in more than one place — centralise and polymorphise it
- The set of products is likely to grow over the lifetime of the project
- You want constructor logic encapsulated (e.g., a Product that requires complex initialisation)

**When NOT to use Factory Method:**
- The product type is singular and will never vary — the pattern adds a layer of indirection with zero benefit
- You have exactly 2-3 types that are completely stable — a simple `if/else` or plain factory function is far easier to read
- Your team is not familiar with the pattern — the indirection (call `createProduct()`, which goes to a subclass, which returns an object) can be confusing for developers who have not seen it before
- You are in a functional codebase where passing factory functions as arguments is idiomatic — the full class hierarchy is cultural overhead

**Real frameworks using it:** React (`createElement`), Node.js (`http.createServer`), NestJS (useFactory providers), Angular (`ComponentFactory`), Mongoose (`model()`), Jest (`jest.fn()`), Spring (`AbstractBeanFactory`), Express (`Router()`).

items: **Factory Method separates creation from use** — the Creator's business logic calls `this.createProduct()` and works against the Product interface; it never sees `new ConcreteProduct()`, so it is unaffected when products change or multiply.
**Polymorphism delivers OCP** — adding a new product type means adding a new ConcreteCreator subclass (and a ConcreteProduct), with zero edits to the Creator, the client, or any existing subclass.

**Simple factory is not Factory Method** — a `switch` in a static function centralises creation but violates OCP; Factory Method distributes the decision across subclasses so no existing code is edited when new types are added.

**Factory Method is a hook inside a Template Method** — the Creator's operation is the template (fixed sequence of steps); `createProduct()` is the overridable hook that subclasses fill in — the two patterns are naturally intertwined and appear together in virtually every framework.

**The JS registry pattern achieves the same goal without deep inheritance** — a `Map<string, () => Product>` satisfies OCP (new entry = new type, no edits) and is more composable, testable, and dynamic than a class hierarchy for most real-world JS/TS applications.

**Watch for the pattern in frameworks you already use** — `React.createElement`, `http.createServer`, NestJS's `useFactory`, Angular's `ComponentFactory`, and Mongoose's `model()` are all Factory Method in production code you likely call every day.

**The smell is scattered `new ConcreteClass()` in business logic** — when you see instantiation decisions (which class to create) mixed into operational logic (what to do with the object), that is the signal: extract to a factory method and let subclasses or a registry make the decision.

quiz.question: What is the PRIMARY structural characteristic that distinguishes the Factory Method pattern from a simple factory function?
options: The factory method always returns an interface type rather than a concrete class.
The factory method is declared in a base class and overridden in subclasses, using polymorphism to decide which product to create.
The factory method is always a static method on the Creator class.
The factory method must accept a type string parameter to determine which object to return.
quiz.explanation: Factory Method is defined by inheritance and polymorphism: the Creator declares the method, ConcreteCreators override it. A simple factory uses a switch/if block in a single function — no subclassing, no polymorphism. Both return interface types, but only Factory Method distributes the decision across subclasses.

quiz.question: A `DocumentConverter` base class has a `createExporter()` method returning an `Exporter` interface. `PdfConverter` and `HtmlConverter` each override it. The client calls `converter.convert(doc)` and never references `PdfExporter` or `HtmlExporter`. Which principle does this most directly demonstrate?
options: Liskov Substitution Principle — subclasses can replace their base class
Open/Closed Principle — the system is open for extension via new subclasses but closed for modification of existing code
Interface Segregation Principle — clients should not depend on methods they do not use
Dependency Inversion Principle — high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules
quiz.explanation: Factory Method's core design goal is OCP: adding a new export format (EpubConverter + EpubExporter) requires zero changes to DocumentConverter, the client, or existing converters. The system is extended without modification. OCP is directly satisfied by the polymorphic dispatch to ConcreteCreator subclasses.

quiz.question: In the Factory Method pattern, `Creator.operate()` calls `this.createProduct()` internally. What additional pattern is `operate()` an example of?
options: Decorator — it wraps the product with additional behaviour
Observer — it notifies the product of state changes
Template Method — it defines a fixed algorithm skeleton with a hook for subclasses
Strategy — it delegates the entire algorithm to an interchangeable object
quiz.explanation: Template Method defines an algorithm skeleton in the base class with 'holes' (abstract methods) for subclasses to fill in. `operate()` is the template — it sequences fixed steps; `createProduct()` is the hook. Factory Method is almost always found inside a Template Method, and the two patterns are naturally intertwined.

quiz.question: You have a JS codebase without class hierarchies. You implement: `const registry = {}; registry['pdf'] = () => new PdfExporter(); registry['html'] = () => new HtmlExporter();`. Adding EPUB requires only `registry['epub'] = () => new EpubExporter()`. Does this satisfy the spirit of Factory Method?
options: No — Factory Method requires class inheritance; a registry object is a simple factory.
No — Factory Method requires the factory function to be declared in a base class.
Yes — the registry satisfies OCP (new type = new entry, no edits) and decouples creation from use, achieving the same goal via a different mechanism.
Yes — but only if the registry is implemented as a class with static methods.
quiz.explanation: The pattern's intent — decouple creation from use and satisfy OCP — is fully achieved by the registry. The mechanism (map vs. inheritance) differs, but the result is the same: client code depends on the product interface, adding a type adds code rather than editing code. In JavaScript, the registry is the idiomatic form of the principle.

quiz.question: Which of the following is the BEST signal that Factory Method should be applied to an existing codebase?
options: A class has more than five public methods.
A switch statement in business logic creates different concrete classes based on a type string, and this pattern recurs in multiple places.
A class constructor takes more than three parameters.
Two classes share a parent class and override the same method.
quiz.explanation: Scattered `switch(type) { case 'X': return new X(); }` in business logic is the canonical Factory Method smell. Each case is a concrete type decision mixed into operational code. Factory Method replaces the switch by making each case a separate ConcreteCreator subclass — business logic just calls the factory method.

quiz.question: What happens to the client code in `processDocuments(converter, docs)` when a new `EpubConverter` class is added to the system?
options: The client must add a new case to handle the EPUB converter type.
The client must be recompiled but no source changes are needed.
The client code is completely unchanged — it works with any DocumentConverter subclass without modification.
The client must update its import statements to include the new converter.
quiz.explanation: This is the central payoff of Factory Method. `processDocuments` depends only on the `DocumentConverter` interface. Adding `EpubConverter` is creating a new class that satisfies that interface — the client never knew about `PdfConverter` or `HtmlConverter` specifically, so it certainly does not need to know about `EpubConverter`. Zero source changes to the client.

quiz.question: In TypeScript, what does marking the factory method as `abstract` in the Creator class accomplish?
options: It makes the method run faster at runtime by skipping virtual dispatch.
It prevents the Creator from being instantiated directly and forces every subclass to implement the factory method — a compile-time guarantee.
It allows the method to return `null` when no product is available.
It means the method can only be called from within the class, not by subclasses.
quiz.explanation: An abstract method in TypeScript (and Java/C#) serves two purposes: it prevents direct instantiation of the abstract class (enforcing that only ConcreteCreators are used), and it guarantees a compile-time error if any subclass forgets to implement the factory method. This turns a potential runtime crash into a build failure — a significant safety improvement.

quiz.question: React's `React.createElement(type, props, children)` is described as a Factory Method. Which aspect of that claim is MOST accurate?
options: It is a Factory Method because it is a static method on the React class.
It is a Factory Method because it creates React element objects (the Product) without callers needing to know or construct the internal element structure directly.
It is a Factory Method because it uses inheritance — JSX subclasses React internally.
It is not a Factory Method — it is a constructor function, which is fundamentally different.
quiz.explanation: createElement is a factory for React element descriptors (the Product). Callers — JSX code — say 'give me an element of this type' without constructing the internal {type, props, children, key, ref, ...} object manually. When React changed its internal representation with Fiber, all JSX code continued working unchanged. That is the factory method's decoupling in action.

quiz.question: A Creator provides a default non-abstract implementation of `createProduct()` that returns a `DefaultProduct`. Subclasses may override it but are not required to. What advantage does this approach offer compared to making it abstract?
options: It is faster at runtime because virtual dispatch is avoided.
It allows the Creator to be used directly (with the default product) while still permitting subclasses to customise — a useful default for framework base classes.
It prevents subclasses from creating incompatible product types.
It means the pattern no longer requires a Product interface.
quiz.explanation: A non-abstract default factory method lets the Creator class itself be instantiated when the default product is acceptable. Framework base classes often use this: most users are happy with the default, but power users subclass and override. The abstract variant is stricter — every user must subclass — which is appropriate when there is no meaningful default.

quiz.question: When is applying the Factory Method pattern OVERKILL and a simpler approach is better?
options: When the product types share a common interface.
When there are more than five product types currently in the system.
When the set of product types is small, stable, and will never grow — a direct `new` call or a two-line if/else is clearer and has less indirection.
When the Creator class has business logic that uses the product.
quiz.explanation: Factory Method's value comes from open-ended extensibility. If you have exactly two product types and both are permanent, the pattern's class hierarchy, abstract method, and polymorphic dispatch are all indirection with no payoff. A simple `if (type === 'pdf') return new PdfExporter()` communicates intent clearly and is trivially testable. Prefer the simplest solution that solves the actual problem.
